steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper proposing to train more robust semantic segmentation models on images generated by a robust label-to-image cGAN. Motivate the robustness and OOD problem, discuss data augmentation and generative models, present our approach, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Semantic segmentation in safety-critical settings and the robustness problem
- Data augmentation and generative models as partial remedies
- Our idea: exploit the symmetry between label-to-image cGANs and segmentation networks
- Challenge: cGANs are not robust to anomalous label maps; Robusta
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Segmentation and robustness
  - used in autonomous driving, medical imaging; safety requirements
  - need accurate segments + reliable predictions under perturbations, distribution shifts, uncommon situations, OOD objects
  - modern DNNs strong on segmentation but generalize poorly to unseen samples: image corruptions, adversarial attacks, change of style
  - overconfident probability estimates even when wrong -> failure modes hard to detect, slows industry adoption
- Remedies so far
  - high-capacity DNNs with uncertainty/calibration awareness could learn such cases if seen in training
  - long-tail samples: extremely numerous, difficult, expensive to acquire
  - data augmentation: perturb input, latent space, output space; bigger and richer training set
  - but not always realistic, often architecture-dependent or unsuitable for segmentation
  - generative models progressing toward abundant high-quality data for data-hungry DNNs
  - excellent FID, yet training on synthetic images non-trivial and less effective than real
  - very recent methods on latest generative models: encouraging for image classification; not yet shown for segmentation with high-resolution images, complex scenes
- Our idea
  - improve robustness to input perturbations and ability to detect outliers (objects with no labels in train set)
  - symmetry: label-to-image cGANs vs image-to-label models to train robust segmentation networks
  - use cGANs at training time to enrich datasets with perturbations and outliers
  - generated data must be good and diverse enough to generalize to unseen real situations, not overfit to training anomalies
- Challenge and Robusta
  - cGANs not robust to input label variations; artifacts on label maps with anomalies
  - Robusta: novel cGAN with attention layers and sub-networks; high-quality images even from corrupted/anomalous label maps
  - Robusta images -> dataset for training an observer network to detect anomalies and failures
- Contributions
  - (1) strategy using cGAN images with outliers to train robust segmentation model (robustness + OOD detection)
  - (2) first framework to evaluate robustness of label-to-image cGANs; multiple cGANs vs three new dataset generation techniques
  - (3) Robusta, cascaded cGAN, more robust than state-of-the-art cGANs on the framework
  - expected to make autonomous driving more reliable and safe via better OOD and failure detection

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is an important perception task and it is commonly used in safety-critical applications like autonomous driving or medical imaging. To meet safety requirements, it is not enough to produce accurate segments, the model also has to make reliable predictions when there are perturbations, distribution shifts, uncommon situations and out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) get impressive performance in segmentation tasks, but they have trouble generalizing to data samples they did not see during training, for example image corruptions, adversarial attacks, or a change of style. When this happens they often give overconfident probability estimates even if they are wrong, and this can make it hard to detect failure modes and so it slows down their adoption in the industry.

In theory, modern high-capacity DNNs trained with uncertainty and calibration awareness could learn to deal with these situations if they had seen them in training. But such samples from the long tail are extremely numerous, and they are difficult and expensive to get in the real world. Since this data is missing, new data augmentation techniques were made to mitigate the problem: they generate perturbations on the input data, the latent space, or the output space. These can help a little with the problem by making the training set bigger with richer samples. Still, the images are not always realistic and the techniques are often architecture-dependent or not suitable for semantic segmentation. At the same time, generative models are making steady progress towards the ambitious goal of generating a lot of high-quality data for training data-hungry DNNs. Even though they have excellent FID scores, training on these synthetic images is non-trivial and less effective than training with real images. Very recent methods based on the latest generative models are starting to show encouraging results for image classification. However, they have not shown yet that they can improve the performance and robustness of semantic segmentation models that deal with high-resolution images and complex scenes.

- Our idea
  - robustness to input perturbations + detecting outliers (objects with no labels in train set)
  - symmetry between label-to-image cGANs and image-to-label models; enrich datasets with perturbations and outliers at training time
  - generated data must be good and diverse enough; no overfitting to training anomalies
- Challenge and Robusta
  - cGANs not robust to label variations; artifacts
  - Robusta: attention layers + sub-networks; good images from corrupted label maps; dataset for an observer network
- Contributions (1) strategy, (2) first evaluation framework, three new dataset generation techniques, (3) Robusta cascaded cGAN; safer autonomous driving

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is an important perception task and it is commonly used in safety-critical applications like autonomous driving or medical imaging. To meet safety requirements, it is not enough to produce accurate segments, the model also has to make reliable predictions when there are perturbations, distribution shifts, uncommon situations and out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) get impressive performance in segmentation tasks, but they have trouble generalizing to data samples they did not see during training, for example image corruptions, adversarial attacks, or a change of style. When this happens they often give overconfident probability estimates even if they are wrong, and this can make it hard to detect failure modes and so it slows down their adoption in the industry.

In theory, modern high-capacity DNNs trained with uncertainty and calibration awareness could learn to deal with these situations if they had seen them in training. But such samples from the long tail are extremely numerous, and they are difficult and expensive to get in the real world. Since this data is missing, new data augmentation techniques were made to mitigate the problem: they generate perturbations on the input data, the latent space, or the output space. These can help a little with the problem by making the training set bigger with richer samples. Still, the images are not always realistic and the techniques are often architecture-dependent or not suitable for semantic segmentation. At the same time, generative models are making steady progress towards the ambitious goal of generating a lot of high-quality data for training data-hungry DNNs. Even though they have excellent FID scores, training on these synthetic images is non-trivial and less effective than training with real images. Very recent methods based on the latest generative models are starting to show encouraging results for image classification. However, they have not shown yet that they can improve the performance and robustness of semantic segmentation models that deal with high-resolution images and complex scenes.

In this paper we want to improve the robustness of semantic segmentation models against input perturbations and also their ability to detect outliers, i.e., objects that have no associated labels in the train set. For this, we propose to use the symmetry between label-to-image conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) and image-to-label models to train robust segmentation networks. We argue that label-to-image cGANs can be used at training time to enrich datasets with perturbations and outliers and so improve segmentation models. The generated data has to be of good enough quality and diversity so that the classifier trained on it can generalize to new and unseen real-world situations, and so that it does not overfit to the specific anomalies of the training set.

A big difficulty is that cGANs are not robust to variations in the input labels. When they get label maps with anomalies they may generate images with artifacts, which makes them less useful for training semantic segmentation. To address this, we propose Robusta, a new cGAN architecture that uses attention layers and sub-networks. Robusta can produce high-quality images even from label maps that have corruptions and anomalies. We use the synthetic images of Robusta to build a dataset for training an observer network that detects anomalies and failures of the segmentation model.

Contributions. (1) We propose a new strategy to improve the robustness and OOD detection performance of semantic segmentation models by using the symmetry of label-to-image cGANs and image-to-label segmentation networks: we train a robust segmentation model with cGAN images with outliers; (2) We design the first framework for evaluating the robustness of label-to-image cGANs against perturbations and uncommon inputs, and with it we investigate the robustness of multiple cGAN methods against three new dataset generation techniques; (3) We propose Robusta, a new cascaded cGAN that is more robust than state-of-the-art cGANs on the proposed framework. We expect our approach to make autonomous driving systems more reliable and safe, because it allows more accurate OOD and failure detection in real-world situations.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is an essential perception task that is commonly used in safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving [1,2] or medical imaging [3,4]. To fulfill safety requirements [5], it is crucial not only to produce accurate segments but also to make reliable predictions in the face of perturbations [6], distribution shifts [7,8,9], uncommon situations [10] and out-of-distribution (OOD) objects [11,12]. Modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) achieve impressive performance in segmentation tasks [13,14,15,16,17]; however, they struggle to generalize to data samples not seen during training, e.g., image corruptions [18,6], adversarial attacks [19,20], or change of style [21]. In such cases, they often produce overconfident probability estimates [22,23,24] even when they are wrong, which can impede the detection of failure modes and thus their adoption in the industry.

Technically, modern high-capacity DNNs trained with uncertainty and calibration awareness could learn to deal with such situations if they were seen during training. However, such samples from the long tail are extremely numerous, difficult, and expensive to acquire in the real world. In the absence of such data, new data augmentation techniques have been devised to mitigate this problem: generating perturbations on the input data [25,26], the latent space [27], or the output space [28]. They may slightly relieve the problem by increasing the size of the training set with richer samples. Still, they do not always yield realistic images and are often architecture-dependent or unsuitable for semantic segmentation. Meanwhile, generative models are making steady progress towards the ambitious goal of generating abundant and high-quality data for training data-hungry DNNs [29,30,31,32]. Despite excellent FID scores [33], training on such synthetic images is non-trivial and less effective than with real images [34,35,36]. Very recent methods based on the latest generative models [37,38] are starting to show encouraging results for image classification. However, they have not yet shown that they can improve the performance and robustness of semantic segmentation models dealing with high-resolution images and complex scenes.

In this paper, we aim to improve the robustness of semantic segmentation models against input perturbations as well as their ability to detect outliers, i.e., objects with no associated labels in the train set. To this end, we propose leveraging the symmetry between label-to-image conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) [39,40] and image-to-label models to train robust segmentation networks [41,42]. We argue that label-to-image cGANs can be used at training time to enrich datasets with perturbations and outliers and thereby improve segmentation models. The generated data must be of sufficient quality and diversity to enable the classifier trained on it to generalize to new and unseen real-world situations and to avoid overfitting to the specific anomalies of the training set.

A significant difficulty is that cGANs are not robust to variations in the input labels: given label maps with anomalies, they may generate images with artifacts, which hinders their utility for semantic segmentation training. To address this challenge, we propose Robusta, a novel cGAN architecture that leverages attention layers [43] and sub-networks [44]. Robusta can produce high-quality images even from label maps with corruptions and anomalies. We exploit Robusta's synthetic images to construct a dataset for training an observer network [45] to detect anomalies and failures of the segmentation model.

Contributions. (1) We propose a new strategy to improve the robustness and OOD detection performance of semantic segmentation models by leveraging the symmetry of label-to-image cGANs and image-to-label segmentation networks: we use cGAN images with outliers to train a robust segmentation model; (2) We design the first framework to evaluate the robustness of label-to-image cGANs against perturbations and uncommon inputs, and we use it to investigate the robustness of multiple cGAN methods against three new dataset generation techniques; (3) We propose Robusta, a new cascaded cGAN with improved robustness compared to state-of-the-art cGANs on the proposed framework. Our approach is expected to make autonomous driving systems more reliable and safe by enabling more accurate OOD and failure detection in real-world situations.
